# PowerShell versions: target, lifecycle, and version-dependent features

> Generated from ai-powershell-standards 2.0.0. Do not edit this file.
> Its source is the `standards` folder of that repository; `Tools/Build-AgentInstructions.ps1` rebuilds it.

These rules apply to every `.ps1`, `.psm1`, and `.psd1` file. They say which PowerShell version to
write for and which features that version has.

The dates and version numbers on this page were checked against Microsoft's documentation, the
PowerShell releases on GitHub, and the .NET release index on 2026-11-17. A version is supported
until its end-of-support date; compare that date with today's date instead of relying on the
wording here.

## Rules

- **VER-01** Write for PowerShell 7.6 (LTS) unless the project declares another target. The
  declaration is the project's `#requires -Version` lines and the `PowerShellVersion` and
  `CompatiblePSEditions` keys of its module manifest.
- **VER-02** Write code that also runs on Windows PowerShell 5.1 only when the project declares it:
  `PowerShellVersion = '5.1'`, `CompatiblePSEditions` containing `Desktop`, or
  `#requires -Version 5.1`.
- **VER-03** Declare the target. A script that is run directly starts with
  `#requires -Version <target>`, and a module manifest sets `PowerShellVersion` and
  `CompatiblePSEditions`. A file that only defines functions for a module or script to load needs no
  `#requires` line. A root module repeats the manifest's version in a `#Requires -Version` line
  (MOD-08).
- **VER-04** Code MUST NOT use a command, parameter, operator, or type that the declared target does
  not have. The feature tables in the PowerShell version rules list the ones that differ.
- **VER-05** Code, `#requires` lines, and CI matrices MUST NOT target a PowerShell version that is
  past its end-of-support date.
- **VER-06** Commands that exist only in Windows PowerShell MUST NOT be used in code that targets
  PowerShell 7: use `Get-CimInstance` in place of `Get-WmiObject`, and `Get-WinEvent` in place of
  `Get-EventLog`.
- **VER-07** Compare versions as `[version]` values, never by `Major` alone, and detect the operating
  system in a way that also works where `$IsWindows` does not exist.
- **VER-08** Install and publish modules with Microsoft.PowerShell.PSResourceGet (`Install-PSResource`,
  `Find-PSResource`, `Publish-PSResource`). Use `Install-Module` only on Windows PowerShell 5.1 where
  PSResourceGet is not installed.
- **VER-09** Detect a parameter that only some versions have on the command itself, with
  `(Get-Command -Name <Command>).Parameters.ContainsKey('<Parameter>')`, not from the version number.
- **VER-10** Code that works on some operating systems only MUST test for them before its first
  platform-specific operation, and fail with an error that names the systems it supports.

## Support lifecycle

| Version | Type | Released | End of support | Runtime |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7.7 | Stable | 10-Nov-2026 | 14-Nov-2028 | .NET 11 |
| 7.6 | LTS | 18-Mar-2026 | 14-Nov-2028 | .NET 10 |
| 7.5 | Stable | 23-Jan-2025 | 10-Nov-2026 | .NET 9 |
| 7.4 | LTS | 16-Nov-2023 | 10-Nov-2026 | .NET 8 |
| 5.1 | Windows component | Aug-2016 | Follows the Windows lifecycle | .NET Framework 4.x |

PowerShell 7.7 is a Stable release, so the default target stays 7.6, the LTS release (VER-01). Both
end support on the same day. Microsoft's lifecycle page did not yet list 7.7 on 2026-11-17: its
release date here is that of the release on GitHub, and its end of support is the date that the
.NET release index gives for .NET 11, which the lifecycle of PowerShell follows.

Versions 6.x and 7.0 to 7.3 ended support earlier. Windows PowerShell 5.1 ships with Windows and is
still supported, but it receives no new features: treat it as a compatibility target, never as the
version to design for.

When a project is pinned to a version whose end-of-support date has passed, say so and recommend
moving to the current LTS. Do not silently change the project's declared target.

## Choosing and declaring a target

| Situation | Target | Manifest keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New automation, CI, containers | 7.6 | `PowerShellVersion = '7.6'`, `CompatiblePSEditions = @('Core')` |
| Module for machines that may not have PowerShell 7 | 5.1 | `PowerShellVersion = '5.1'`, `CompatiblePSEditions = @('Desktop', 'Core')` |
| Code that needs a feature added in 7.7 | 7.7 | `PowerShellVersion = '7.7'`, `CompatiblePSEditions = @('Core')` |

```powershell
#requires -Version 7.6
```

When the project declares no target and it is not clear which row applies, ask before generating
code. If the question cannot be asked, VER-01 applies: write for 7.6 and say that the target was
assumed.

PowerShell 7.7 is opt-in. Use a feature that 7.7 added only when the project declares 7.7, with
`#requires -Version 7.7` or `PowerShellVersion = '7.7'`; without that declaration the target is 7.6
(VER-01, VER-04). Code written for 7.6 is also run on 7.7 by anyone who has installed it, so check
it against the behaviour that 7.7 changed, which is listed below.

`#requires -Version 7.0` is obsolete, because that version is retired. To say "any PowerShell 7",
name the lowest supported version: 7.6 since 10-Nov-2026, when 7.4 and 7.5 left support.

A module that targets 5.1 gates each command that only PowerShell 7 has behind a version check
(VER-07), or a test of the command for a parameter (VER-09), and gives 5.1 the replacement from the
table below. Syntax cannot be gated: a file that contains 7-only syntax does not parse on 5.1,
whichever branch would run.

## Features by version

### Not available in Windows PowerShell 5.1

Code that must run on 5.1 MUST NOT use these:

| Feature | Use on 5.1 |
| --- | --- |
| Ternary `a ? b : c`, `??`, `??=`, `?.`, `?[]` | `if` / `else` |
| Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `\|\|` | Separate statements that test `$?` or `$LASTEXITCODE` |
| `ForEach-Object -Parallel` | `Start-Job`, a runspace pool, sequential code, or the ThreadJob module installed separately |
| `$IsWindows`, `$IsLinux`, `$IsMacOS` | See operating system detection below |
| `Join-Path` with more than one child path | Nested `Join-Path` calls |
| `-Encoding utf8NoBOM` | `[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText()` with `[System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)` |
| `ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable` | Read properties from the object that `ConvertFrom-Json` returns |
| `Test-Json` | `ConvertFrom-Json` inside `try` / `catch` |
| `Get-Content -AsByteStream` | `Get-Content -Encoding Byte` |
| `[ValidateNotNullOrWhiteSpace()]` | `[ValidateScript({ -not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($_) })]` |
| `clean { }` block, `Get-Error`, `$PSStyle` | No equivalent; use `try` / `finally` in place of `clean` |
| `Invoke-WebRequest` without `-UseBasicParsing` | Pass `-UseBasicParsing` in unattended code |
| `-SkipHttpErrorCheck`, and other parameters added in PowerShell 7 | Test for the parameter on the command (VER-09) |

One use of 7-only syntax in any file that a root module dot-sources fails the whole import on 5.1,
so one helper can take every command of the module with it.

### Added in PowerShell 7.5

| Feature | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `ConvertTo-CliXml`, `ConvertFrom-CliXml` | Serialize to CLIXML text without a temporary file |
| `ConvertFrom-Json -DateKind` | Controls how date strings are converted (`Local`, `Utc`, `Offset`, `String`). Use `Utc` or `Offset` for audit data. |
| `Test-Json -Options IgnoreComments, AllowTrailingCommas` | Validates JSON that has comments or trailing commas |
| `Resolve-Path -Force`, `Convert-Path -Force` | Wildcard resolution that includes hidden items |
| `New-Guid -Empty`, `New-Guid -InputObject` | An empty GUID, and conversion of a string to a GUID |
| `Get-Process -IncludeUserName` | No longer needs elevation on Windows |
| Error `ConciseView` | Shows the `RecommendedAction` of an error, on a `Recommendation:` line |

### Added in PowerShell 7.6

| Feature | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `Get-Command -ExcludeModule` | Leaves out commands from the named modules |
| `Get-Clipboard -Delimiter` | Splits clipboard text while reading it |
| `Register-ArgumentCompleter -NativeFallback` | One completer for native commands that have none |
| `.PSForEach()`, `.PSWhere()` | Aliases for the `.ForEach()` and `.Where()` intrinsic methods. Prefer them when `.ForEach()` or `.Where()` collides with a method of the object's own type, as `.ForEach()` does on a `List[T]`. |
| Redirection to a variable | `Get-Item -LiteralPath $path 2>&1 > variable:itemResult` |
| `PipelineStopToken` on `Cmdlet` | For binary cmdlets: a `CancellationToken` that is signalled when the pipeline stops |

### Added in PowerShell 7.7

Code that targets 7.6 MUST NOT use these (VER-04). Each was run on PowerShell 7.7.0 and is absent
from PowerShell 7.6.10 and Windows PowerShell 5.1. A comparison of every command and parameter that
7.6.10 and 7.7.0 ship found nothing else added outside PSResourceGet, and nothing removed.

| Feature | Use on 7.6 |
| --- | --- |
| `New-TemporaryDirectory` | `[System.IO.Directory]::CreateTempSubdirectory()`. On 5.1, `New-Item -ItemType Directory` with a path made from `[System.IO.Path]::GetTempPath()` and `[System.IO.Path]::GetRandomFileName()`. |
| `Join-Path -Extension` | `[System.IO.Path]::ChangeExtension()` on the joined path. With an empty extension it leaves the dot, as in `file.`, where `-Extension ''` removes the dot too. |
| `-ExcludeProperty` on `Format-Table`, `Format-List`, `Format-Wide`, and `Format-Custom` | `Select-Object -Property * -ExcludeProperty <names>` before the formatting command |
| `[WildcardPattern]::ToRegex()` | Match with the pattern's own `IsMatch()` method |
| `$PSApplicationOutputEncoding`, the encoding used to read the output of a native executable | Set `[Console]::OutputEncoding`, and restore it in `finally` |

Assigning `$PSApplicationOutputEncoding` on 7.6 raises no error and changes nothing: it creates an
ordinary variable, and the output is still read with `[Console]::OutputEncoding`.

### Promoted from experimental

These features are always on from the version shown. Do not tell users to enable them with
`Enable-ExperimentalFeature`.

| Version | Features |
| --- | --- |
| 7.5 | `PSCommandNotFoundSuggestion`, `PSCommandWithArgs`, `PSModuleAutoLoadSkipOfflineFiles` |
| 7.6 | `PSFeedbackProvider`, `PSNativeWindowsTildeExpansion`, `PSRedirectToVariable`, `PSSubsystemPluginModel` |

`PSRedirectToVariable` is the redirection to a variable in the table above.

PowerShell 7.7 promotes no feature. `PSLoadAssemblyFromNativeCode`,
`PSSerializeJSONLongEnumAsNumber`, and `PSProfileDSCResource` are still experimental in it.

### Behaviour that changed

Code MUST NOT depend on the older behaviour.

Each row for 7.7 was measured on PowerShell 7.7.0, and the older behaviour on PowerShell 7.6.10 and
Windows PowerShell 5.1. The rows for 7.6.5, 7.6.7, and 7.6.10 are servicing releases of 7.6: they
were measured on 7.6.10, and 7.7.0 behaves the same way.

| Version | Change |
| --- | --- |
| 7.7 | `New-Guid` returns a version 7 UUID, which begins with the time it was created. Earlier versions return a random version 4 UUID. Where the kind matters, call `[guid]::NewGuid()` for version 4, or `[guid]::CreateVersion7()` for version 7, which Windows PowerShell 5.1 does not have. A GUID identifies something; it is not a secret, and from 7.7 part of it can be worked out from the time. |
| 7.7 | `-NoTypeInformation` on `Export-Csv` and `ConvertTo-Csv` is obsolete: it has no effect, and it writes a warning each time it is passed. Windows PowerShell 5.1 still writes a `#TYPE` line without it. See the note on CSV type information below. |
| 7.7 | `Export-Csv -Append -NoHeader` is a terminating error. On 7.6 the pair is accepted and writes the rows without a header. |
| 7.7 | `Format-Table`, `Format-List`, and `Format-Custom` reject `-Property $null` and an empty array. Earlier versions accept `$null` and show every property. Add the parameter to a splat only when it has a value. |
| 7.7 | `Get-ChildItem -Path '*.md' -Recurse -Name` also returns the matches in subfolders. On 7.6 and 5.1 it returns only those in the starting folder, while `-Filter '*.md'` recurses on every version (STY-43). |
| 7.7 | `Resolve-Path -Relative` writes `.\.config\app.json` for a name that starts with a dot. On 7.6 and 5.1 it writes `.config\app.json`. |
| 7.7 | `Get-Help` prints the `.NOTES` text one blank line below its heading and indented by four spaces, like the other sections. On 7.6 and 5.1 there are two blank lines and eight spaces, so a test that compares help text exactly gets a different result. |
| 7.6.10 | `New-FileCatalog -CatalogVersion 1`, and `Test-FileCatalog` on a version 1 catalog, write a warning, because version 1 uses SHA-1. Windows PowerShell 5.1 (build 26100) writes one too. |
| 7.6.7 | `Test-Json` fetches a schema that another schema refers to by URL only when `-FetchExternalReference` is passed. Without it the reference is an error, `UnresolvedJsonSchemaRef`, and the result is `$false` for valid input as well. |
| 7.6.5 | `Invoke-RestMethod` and `Invoke-WebRequest` send the `Authorization` header with the first request only. A link followed by `-FollowRelLink` is requested without it, as the target of a redirect is, unless `-PreserveAuthorizationOnRedirect` is passed. A function that sends a credential follows the links itself (SEC-09). |
| 7.6 | The `ThreadJob` module is now `Microsoft.PowerShell.ThreadJob`. Call `Start-ThreadJob` without a module prefix; `ThreadJob\Start-ThreadJob` and a `RequiredModules` entry for `ThreadJob` no longer resolve. Where a prefix or an entry is needed, write `Microsoft.PowerShell.ThreadJob\Start-ThreadJob` and `@{ ModuleName = 'Microsoft.PowerShell.ThreadJob'; ModuleVersion = '2.2.0' }`. |
| 7.6 | `Join-Path -ChildPath` accepts an array. An array that used to be joined into one segment is now treated as several segments. |
| 7.6 | `[WildcardPattern]::Escape()` escapes a lone backtick correctly. Code that escaped twice to work around the old result now escapes too much. |
| 7.5 | `ConvertTo-Json` writes a `BigInteger` as a number, not as an object. |
| 7.5 | `Test-Path -OlderThan` and `-NewerThan` both apply when used together. Before, `-OlderThan` was silently ignored, so a date-range check that appeared to work was not filtering. |
| 7.5 | `New-FileCatalog -CatalogVersion` defaults to 2. Pass `-CatalogVersion 1` when a downstream validator still requires version 1. |
| 7.5 | `Select-String` returns `LineNumber` as `[ulong]`. |
| 7.4 | `Test-Json` accepts only strictly valid JSON and no longer supports Draft 4 schemas. |

**CSV type information.** On 7.7.0 each call that passes the switch writes
`Parameter 'NoTypeInformation' is obsolete`, followed by the reason. Code that also runs on Windows
PowerShell 5.1 passes the switch only there:

```powershell
$exportParameters = @{
    LiteralPath = $csvPath
    Encoding = 'utf8'
}
if ($PSVersionTable.PSVersion -lt [version]'6.0') {
    # Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes a #TYPE line unless this switch is passed.
    $exportParameters['NoTypeInformation'] = $true
}
$rows | Export-Csv @exportParameters
```

Run on PowerShell 7.7.0, PowerShell 7.6.10, and Windows PowerShell 5.1: no warning, and the file
starts with the header line on all three.

### Windows PowerShell commands that are not part of PowerShell 7 (VER-06)

| Do not use | Use instead |
| --- | --- |
| `Get-WmiObject`, `Invoke-WmiMethod`, `Set-WmiInstance`, `Remove-WmiObject`, `Register-WmiEvent` | `Get-CimInstance`, `Invoke-CimMethod`, `Set-CimInstance`, `Remove-CimInstance`, `Register-CimIndicationEvent` |
| `Get-EventLog`, `Write-EventLog`, `New-EventLog`, `Clear-EventLog` | `Get-WinEvent`; `New-WinEvent` to write an event for a registered provider |
| `New-WebServiceProxy` | `Invoke-RestMethod`, or a generated client |
| `Add-PSSnapin`, workflows, `*-Transaction` | Modules; no equivalent for workflows and transactions |

On Windows, some of these still resolve in PowerShell 7 through the Windows PowerShell compatibility
session. That path is slow, exists only on Windows, and returns deserialized objects without methods,
so do not rely on it. `Send-MailMessage` exists in PowerShell 7 but is obsolete; do not use it in new
code.

### Behaviour that differs on Windows PowerShell 5.1

None of these raises a parse error. Each was measured on PowerShell 7.6 and Windows PowerShell 5.1.

| Area | PowerShell 7.6 | Windows PowerShell 5.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Group-Object` | Groups are sorted by name | Groups keep the order in which they first appear |
| `.Count` on a `[PSCustomObject]` | `1` | `$null`, or an error under strict mode |
| `[System.IO.Compression.ZipFile]::CreateFromDirectory()` | Entry names use `/` | Entry names use `\` |
| `[System.Net.HttpStatusCode]` | Defines 429 | Does not define 429 |
| A 4xx or 5xx reply to `Invoke-WebRequest` | Returned when `-SkipHttpErrorCheck` is passed | Thrown as a `WebException` |

Sort explicitly before relying on the order of groups. Build an archive entry by entry, with `/` in
the names, when it must open on another platform. Read an HTTP status as an integer, not by name.

A statement used as an expression enumerates its output on both versions. A `WebHeaderCollection`
assigned from an `if` expression therefore arrives as an array of its key names; assign it inside
the branch instead.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 uses `[System.Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol`. Where that is
`SystemDefault`, the operating system chooses the protocols and the code should leave it alone:
adding `Tls12` with `-bor` to `SystemDefault` restricts the session to TLS 1.2. Add `Tls12` only when
the value names specific protocols and TLS 1.2 is not one of them.

### Reading a failed HTTP reply on both versions (VER-09)

On PowerShell 7, `-SkipHttpErrorCheck` returns a 4xx or 5xx reply like any other. Windows PowerShell
5.1 has no such parameter: the cmdlet throws a `WebException`, and the reply is on the exception.
The function below gives callers one error on both versions and was run against a local server on
each. On 5.1 the body came back empty until the stream was moved back to its start.

```powershell
# Detected once, when the module is imported
$script:canSkipHttpErrorCheck = (Get-Command -Name Invoke-WebRequest).Parameters.ContainsKey('SkipHttpErrorCheck')


function Invoke-ModuleWebRequest {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([string])]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [hashtable]$Request
    )

    try {
        if ($script:canSkipHttpErrorCheck) {
            $response = Invoke-WebRequest @Request -SkipHttpErrorCheck -ErrorAction Stop
        } else {
            $response = Invoke-WebRequest @Request -UseBasicParsing -ErrorAction Stop
        }
        $status = [int]$response.StatusCode
        $body = $response.Content
    } catch [System.Net.WebException] {
        $failedResponse = $_.Exception.Response
        if ($null -eq $failedResponse) {
            # No reply arrived, so there is no status or body to read.
            $PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError($_)
        }

        $status = [int]$failedResponse.StatusCode
        # The cmdlet may already have read the reply, so start again from the beginning.
        $stream = $failedResponse.GetResponseStream()
        if ($stream.CanSeek) {
            $stream.Position = 0
        }
        $reader = [System.IO.StreamReader]::new($stream)
        try {
            $body = $reader.ReadToEnd()
        } finally {
            $reader.Dispose()
        }
    } catch {
        $PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError($_)
    }

    if ($status -ge 400) {
        $requestUri = ([uri]$Request['Uri']).GetLeftPart([System.UriPartial]::Path)
        $exception = [System.InvalidOperationException]::new("HTTP $status from $requestUri.")
        $exception.Data['Body'] = $body
        $category = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorCategory]::InvalidResult
        $errorRecord = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]::new(
            $exception, 'HttpRequestFailed', $category, $status)
        $PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError($errorRecord)
    }

    $body
}
```

The message names the status and the request URI. The URI is written without its query string,
which can carry a token, and the body goes into the exception's `Data`, not into the message,
because a reply can carry personal data (SEC-06).

## Detecting the version and operating system (VER-07, VER-10)

```powershell
# Compliant: compares the whole version
if ($PSVersionTable.PSVersion -ge [version]'7.6') {
    $delimitedText = Get-Clipboard -Delimiter ','
}

# Compliant: $IsWindows does not exist on Windows PowerShell 5.1, which runs only on Windows
$onWindows = $PSVersionTable.PSVersion.Major -lt 6 -or $IsWindows

# Non-compliant: true for every 7.x release, supported or not
if ($PSVersionTable.PSVersion.Major -ge 7) {
    $delimitedText = Get-Clipboard -Delimiter ','
}
```

**VER-10.** Test at the start of the function or script, before anything platform-specific runs:

```powershell
$onWindows = $PSVersionTable.PSVersion.Major -lt 6 -or $IsWindows
if (-not $onWindows) {
    $exception = [System.PlatformNotSupportedException]::new('Get-ServiceReport requires Windows.')
    $category = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorCategory]::NotImplemented
    $errorRecord = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]::new(
        $exception, 'UnsupportedOperatingSystem', $category, $null)
    $PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError($errorRecord)
}
```

The test also runs under strict mode on Windows PowerShell 5.1, where `$IsWindows` does not exist:
`-or` does not evaluate its right side when the left side is true.

Report the .NET runtime when diagnosing behaviour that differs by platform. The value starts with
`.NET 10` on PowerShell 7.6 and with `.NET Framework 4.8` on Windows PowerShell 5.1:

```powershell
[System.Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation]::FrameworkDescription
```

## Installing modules (VER-08)

```powershell
Install-PSResource -Name Pester -Version 6.2.0 -Scope CurrentUser -TrustRepository
```

Microsoft.PowerShell.PSResourceGet is included with PowerShell 7.4 and later. PowerShellGet 2.2.5
still ships with PowerShell 7.6, so `Install-Module` and `Find-Module` still exist there, but new
instructions use the PSResourceGet commands. On Windows PowerShell 5.1 PSResourceGet has to be
installed first, so a script that must bootstrap on both checks for it:

```powershell
if (Get-Command -Name Install-PSResource -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
    Install-PSResource -Name $moduleName -Scope CurrentUser -TrustRepository
} else {
    Install-Module -Name $moduleName -Scope CurrentUser -Force -SkipPublisherCheck
}
```

`-SkipPublisherCheck` is needed when Windows ships an older copy of the module under another
publisher, as it ships Pester 3.4.0.
